ami_style_notes:
The meeting has a warm, informal video-call style with medium-to-long presentation turns and mostly short, fragmented discussion turns. Early conversation is loose and social, with frequent greetings, repeated acknowledgments (“yeah,” “okay,” “great”), technical check-ins, and occasional overlap or abrupt handoffs; the transcript also contains many false starts, self-corrections, repeated words, and nonnative-sounding phrasing. Speakers hedge heavily in questions and answers with “um,” “I think,” “sort of,” “maybe,” “you know,” and disclaimers such as calling a question “naive” or noting uncertainty. During talks, speakers become more structured and explanatory, using rhetorical questions, signposting, and recap statements, while the Q&A returns to exploratory, collaborative exchanges. Challenges are indirect and respectful: participants frame alternatives as questions, acknowledge good points first, and describe limitations rather than bluntly disputing claims. Questions are often multipart, conversationally built in real time, and followed by clarifications or restatements when the respondent does not immediately address the intended point.

Meeting style for this meeting (round_robin_updates): Each person takes a turn reporting what they have done since last time. Updates are fairly long and mostly uninterrupted. There are a few clarifying questions between updates and little cross-talk. The discussion that does happen is brief.
Illustration of the feel only (invented, do not reuse the wording or topic):
  - Okay, mine. I got through most of the interviews, I think fourteen of twenty, and the rest are scheduled for the following two weeks.
  - Fourteen, nice. Were those all from the first batch?
  - Most of them. A couple were referrals.
Opening: Start with one person already reading from, or referring to, a document the others have open.
Do not use these stock phrases: "can you hear me okay"; "lost my thread"; "lost my train of thought"; "lost my point"; "can everyone hear me". The recording does not need to begin with audio or login checks.
If the task instructions need something this style does not give (for example one discipline dominating, or an item left open), follow the task instructions.
research_problem: Judging whether a headband neurofeedback program improves attention in elementary classrooms.

speakers.name: Dr. Maya Chen
speakers.background: Dr. Chen is a cognitive neuroscientist with 12 years of experience studying EEG markers of sustained attention and self-regulation in children. She has led school-based neurofeedback studies using behavioral attention tasks, classroom observation protocols, and repeated EEG recordings, with particular attention to expectancy effects and the difference between changes in device-derived metrics and meaningful behavioral change.
speakers.distinct_perspective: Chen treats the headband's attention score as a measurement and intervention claim that must be validated against observable attention, not accepted at face value. She will press for baseline and week-10 EEG and behavioral measures, standardized procedures that limit novelty and placebo/expectation effects, and a later follow-up to distinguish a short-lived training effect from durable change. As project manager, she will keep the matched usual-instruction comparison, assessment schedule, and interpretation criteria aligned before the October 6 deployment target.
speakers.language_complexity: moderate — balances jargon with accessible language

speakers.name: Luis Romero
speakers.background: Luis Romero has 15 years of experience as an elementary instructional coach and district-university partnership coordinator. His work centers on grades 3-5 classroom implementation, teacher professional learning, curriculum-aligned student outcomes, and participation patterns across classrooms serving different language, disability, and socioeconomic groups. He routinely uses teacher interviews, brief lesson logs, student work, classroom observations, and practical implementation feedback to judge whether an instructional program can survive ordinary school routines.
speakers.distinct_perspective: Romero defines success in terms teachers and students can actually experience: whether the program fits regular lessons, whether it displaces valuable instruction, whether teachers can use it consistently after orientation, and whether participation is equitable across matched classrooms. He will advocate for baseline and week-10 learning and classroom-attention measures, teacher usability logs, a short pre-deployment orientation, and clear procedures that do not make participation depend on which classroom has more time, staffing, or familiarity with technology.
speakers.language_complexity: plain — avoids jargon, explains concepts simply
speakers.epistemic_stance: uncertain about how their methods apply to this problem

speakers.name: Priya Nair
speakers.background: Priya Nair is a biomedical engineer with 10 years of experience evaluating wearable biosensors in pediatric and community settings. She has overseen dry-electrode EEG validation, fit testing across child head sizes and hair types, artifact characterization, electrical and skin-safety checks, infection-control workflows, charging logistics, and battery stress testing. Her prior deployments have included classroom-scale device inventories where reliability depends as much on handling and maintenance routines as on laboratory specifications.
speakers.distinct_perspective: Nair views the pilot as dependent on a reliable measurement chain: a headband must fit safely, maintain acceptable electrode contact, record usable signal during ordinary movement, survive cleaning between children, and remain powered for the intended lesson window. She will require device acceptance checks before October 6, including child fit trials, signal-quality thresholds, charging and battery-runtime verification, cleaning procedures, spare-device planning, and a simple troubleshooting path for teachers. She will distinguish missing or poor-quality EEG data from true changes in attention.
speakers.language_complexity: high jargon — uses discipline-specific terminology freely

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Chen
transcript.text: I’m looking at the draft timeline in the shared document, and October 6 is closer than it looks. Before we get into the details, I’d like us to leave today clear on the minimum protocol we need for a credible pilot. That means the matched comparison classrooms, baseline and week-10 assessments, and what has to be true on the device side before children use these in lessons. I hope everyone had a reasonably quiet start to the school year.

transcript.speaker: Priya Nair
transcript.text: On the device side, I need the acceptance checks done before October 6, not just a bench check. We need to- I need to see child fit across head sizes and hair types, sustained signal-quality verification during actual seated work, electrical and skin-safety, a cleaning and charging workflow, battery runtime, and enough spares for units we pull out of service. Otherwise missing EEG will get folded into an attention result, and that would be a pretty serious interpretive error.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Chen
transcript.text: Exactly. Priya, for interpretation, I need to know what the signal-quality trace looks like during ordinary movement. If apparent score gains- if they coincide with worsening or selectively missing data, we can't call that improved attention. Could your acceptance checks give us a threshold for when a classroom session is too ambiguous to include?

transcript.speaker: Priya Nair
transcript.text: I wouldn't set that from the first clean startup minute. I'd keep electrode-contact quality by channel, impedance or the vendor's contact proxy if that's all it exposes, packet loss, motion and artifact flags, and the proportion of usable epochs across the whole lesson. Then we can define a session-level exclusion rule and a child-level missingness flag. We've already seen two apparently good fits lose contact several minutes into quiet work, so the threshold- sustained performance has to be part of it.

transcript.speaker: Luis Romero
transcript.text: Mm, over the whole lesson.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Chen
transcript.text: I’d treat those quality fields as part of the outcome record, not just engineering metadata. If a child’s score rises while usable epochs fall, or missingness differs by classroom or by week, that’s not interpretable as improved attention. We need the exclusion rule fixed before baseline, or rather, before we see results.

transcript.speaker: Priya Nair
transcript.text: Yeah, that has to be fixed.

transcript.speaker: Luis Romero
transcript.text: Alongside that, I’d want the use record fixed too, just a very short teacher log of whether the session happened, how long it actually ran, and why it was shortened or skipped. Teachers can say a routine feels easy, but assemblies and intervention groups can quietly knock out half the uses, so otherwise we won’t know what we’re comparing.

transcript.speaker: Priya Nair
transcript.text: And the reason code needs to separate a skipped session from a device failure. Low battery, failed contact, cleaning turnaround, whatever, that's different from a classroom interruption. Otherwise we'll call it an implementation problem when it's actually a headband reliability problem. Luis, what storage and handoff pattern do you think is realistic without making somebody stay after school to manage chargers?

transcript.speaker: Luis Romero
transcript.text: It has to sit inside the existing classroom routine, not have a teacher taking a box home every night. Maybe there’s a labeled charging station in the classroom or one shared nearby, with one designated school-day handoff. Though I’d want to ask principals who can actually own that. If charging or cleaning adds even, say, ten minutes at dismissal, it’s going to- it’ll become uneven pretty fast.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Chen
transcript.text: Hm, principals will know.

transcript.speaker: Priya Nair
transcript.text: I’d rather not design around a teacher-owned end-of-day task at all. We need to verify the actual inventory first, headbands, dedicated chargers, and spares, because a shared station only works if a low-battery or failed-contact unit can be quarantined without reducing that day’s session capacity. I’m not sure we have that margin...

transcript.speaker: Luis Romero
transcript.text: That inventory question affects fairness too. If one room has enough working units and another is regularly down a few, participation starts tracking equipment luck, or which teacher has time to troubleshoot, not the program. Do we know yet if the intended routine is the whole class at once or a smaller rotating group? That changes what a missed unit means.

transcript.speaker: Priya Nair
transcript.text: That has to be explicit before I can size the readiness test. If it's whole-class simultaneous use, I need enough validated units, chargers, and probably a small quarantine pool on site. If it's a rotating group, the battery and cleaning cycle changes completely. Luis, do the teachers already have a preference, or is that still open?

transcript.speaker: Luis Romero
transcript.text: It’s still open. I wouldn’t assume whole-class is workable just because it’s cleaner for the study. Teachers may prefer a small rotating group if the fitting and transition time is real. But then we need to be careful that the same kinds of kids aren’t always the ones who get a- who get a turn. I can ask the principals and teachers what lesson window they could protect, and whether they see whole-class or rotation as less disruptive.

transcript.speaker: Priya Nair
transcript.text: From the hardware side, I’d strongly prefer we not choose the delivery model just on convenience. A rotating group may make fit and cleaning manageable, but it creates more repeated donning, more opportunities for contact loss, and a different battery-duty cycle. Whole-class use- that stresses inventory and charging instead. Once Luis gets the teacher view, I can run the acceptance test against the actual workflow rather than a hypothetical one.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Chen
transcript.text: The delivery model also changes what our comparison means. If it's a rotating group, we need to specify an equitable selection process and schedule ahead of time, not have teachers informally choose the children they think most need attention support. And we should record each child's actual exposure. I'd rather wait for Luis's teacher input before we treat either format as the study protocol.

transcript.speaker: Luis Romero
transcript.text: And I’d want that schedule visible enough that we can check it, not just ask teachers afterward who got sessions. I’ll find out whether principals can protect a consistent window without taking from required literacy or math, or- without taking time from required literacy or math, because if the answer is no, that may decide the format before we get too far into it.

transcript.speaker: Priya Nair
transcript.text: That teacher input is the gating item for the engineering plan too. I can't certify battery runtime or cleaning turnaround in the abstract. With rotation, we need to stress-test repeated fit, wipe-down, and reissue cycles. With simultaneous use, we validate the full charging bay and reserve pool. I also still need to check whether our current inventory supports either one without borrowing capacity from another classroom.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Chen
transcript.text: And until we fix the format, I wouldn’t finalize the assessment schedule either. We need a baseline before any headband exposure, then the same brief behavioral attention measure and EEG procedure at week 10 in both the participating and matched usual-instruction classrooms, and then a later follow-up. Otherwise, a novelty-related change can look like an effect. I’m still checking whether the task we selected is short enough for grades 3 through 5 without getting too, uh, unreliable when we repeat it.

transcript.speaker: Priya Nair
transcript.text: For that baseline procedure, Maya, I need the same sustained-quality fields captured in both arms, even if the usual-instruction children never use the intervention during lessons. Otherwise, a grade or hair-type difference in dry-electrode contact can masquerade as a between-group EEG difference. And once you know the candidate task duration, I can tell you- I can check whether it fits inside the battery and contact-stability test window.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Chen
transcript.text: Yes, both arms.

transcript.speaker: Luis Romero
transcript.text: And for the classroom side, baseline and week 10 should include something teachers can recognize too, not just the EEG task. Maybe the same brief observation or attention rating during a regular lesson, plus a small learning check tied to whatever block the routine sits in. Maya, once you've narrowed the task, what size of change, change would you consider meaningful in a way a teacher might actually notice?

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Chen
transcript.text: I wouldn't set a meaningful threshold from the headband score itself. I'd want to see convergence, with a pre-specified improvement on the behavioral task and, ideally, a modest but observable increase in on-task behavior during the regular lesson compared with the matched classrooms. And for the learning check, Luis, I think it needs to be brief and common enough across rooms so we're not accidentally measuring whose curriculum happened to line up with the intervention window.

transcript.speaker: Priya Nair
transcript.text: That sounds right, but the observation protocol needs to log whether a child was actually wearing a device and whether that recording was usable. Otherwise, we could see an apparent association between on-task behavior and a headband score that is really just selective contact failure. I’ll wait for the task duration and delivery format, then set the sustained-contact and runtime acceptance window around the real lesson, not the lab- not a lab surrogate.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Chen
transcript.text: I think we're at the point where we shouldn't promise October 6 is fixed until we know the delivery format and inventory. Luis, if you can get the protected-window and format information quickly, we can lock in the matched classrooms and baseline procedures around it. And meanwhile I'll verify the repeated-task reliability and draft standardized assessment language for both arms. I don't want to- so we're not cueing one group to expect an attention benefit.

transcript.speaker: Priya Nair
transcript.text: I agree. October 6 is contingent on a documented readiness gate. We need the format and inventory confirmed, then fit, sustained contact, safety, cleaning, charging, and battery checks in that actual workflow. If the inventory or contact stability fails, I don't think we should quietly proceed and call it a pilot of attention.

transcript.speaker: Luis Romero
transcript.text: I’ll get the principals’ read on a protected window, whether it’s likely to be whole-class or rotation, and who can own the day-to-day handoff. I’ll also make sure we hear from rooms with less staffing or less comfort with the tech, not just the early adopters. Then we can tell whether October 6 is a real date or just, you know, the date on the calendar...

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Chen
transcript.text: Given the hard stop, October 6 can't be assumed. Once we have Luis's format information and Priya's readiness result, I can finalize the matched comparison and the baseline, week-10, and follow-up assessment plan. And we shouldn't- there shouldn't be any interpretation of an attention benefit unless the behavioral and observation measures move in the same direction.

transcript.speaker: Priya Nair
transcript.text: Okay, I think we've covered what we needed today. Thanks, everyone. Once the format information is back, we can reconvene and see where the readiness checks are- stand.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Chen
transcript.text: Thank you. Goodbye, everyone.
